testCases.input: Compare model evals vs app evals in LLM testing: scope, goals, and metrics.
testCases.actualOutput:
Scope
- Model evals: Test the LLM itself — its raw capabilities as a model. Used when a new LLM is released to benchmark and document model-level performance.
- Application evals: Test LLM-based applications — the system built around the LLM (how it behaves inside an app or product).

Goals
- Model evals: Determine and benchmark the model’s capabilities (e.g., which leaderboard/benchmark it tops). Provide a documented capability level for the model.
- Application evals: Judge the behavior and suitability of the full LLM-powered application in its intended use (how the model+app perform together).
- Shared goal: Not merely to produce a single score, but to answer practical questions about what is being tested, when, and how.

Metrics / What you measure
- Model evals: Metrics focus on model capability and benchmark performance (example given: accuracy of the retriever), using prepared datasets and chosen evaluation tools.
- Application evals: Metrics are tied to the application use case and the full testing setup (what you test, which data, when you run tests, and which tools). Specific application metrics aren’t listed in the lecture, but are chosen based on the app’s requirements and setup.

Overall takeaway
- “LLM evals” refers to the entire testing setup (what, why, when, and which tools), and can mean either model evals or application evals depending on the use case.

testCases.name: test_case_1
testCases.input: How do ML systems and LLM apps differ in determinism, dynamic cost, and input-output tracking?
testCases.actualOutput:
- Determinism:
  - ML systems: outputs are deterministic. Given the same input (like 2 and 3 to a calculator) you always get the same exact output (5). Evaluation is simple and automated with mathematical formulas or pass/fail tests.
  - LLM apps: outputs are probabilistic and non-deterministic. The same input can produce different, valid outputs (different words, sentence counts, lengths). Simple assertion-based testing fails because there is no single correct string.

- Dynamic cost:
  - ML systems: cost is predictable per dataset/compute. Example from the lecture: 100 rows always cost 10 rupees when hosted on a server.
  - LLM apps: cost is dynamic and hard to fix because both input length and output length drive cost. Input cost and output cost vary per request, so overall cost is difficult to judge.

- Input–output tracking and evaluation:
  - ML systems: relationship between input and output is static and easy to manage; evaluation is cheap and automated.
  - LLM apps: relationship is dynamic — nothing is fixed; outputs are semantically flexible (not exact strings), multiple components (e.g., retriever and generator) can fail independently, and evaluation is costly (text requires detailed, often human judgment). Human annotation doesn’t scale, so you need careful automated or hybrid evaluation approaches and ongoing management of input/output behavior.
testCases.expectedOutput:
ML systems are generally deterministic: the same input row gives the same output every time, with fixed compute/cost for that input size.  

LLM apps are probabilistic and dynamic: the same input can produce different outputs, and both cost and compute vary because input length, output length, and retrieved context all change.  

Also, ML prediction usually has a simple input-to-output flow, while LLM apps often require tracking the full journey from input through retrieval, prompting, and output.

- Generator ignoring the retrieved context and producing wrong answers (i.e., not grounding its output on the given context).

- Agentic/autonomous behavior / silent interpretation: in more autonomous systems hallucinations can occur and be harder to see and correct because the model acts without visible, correctable outputs.

- Traditional cybersecurity (problem-finding):
  - Focuses on discovering vulnerabilities and bugs in code or systems.
  - Often depends on human-driven reporting and volunteer contributions: people find bugs, send fixes to maintainers, and those maintainers decide whether to accept them.
  - Largely reactive: you find a problem first, then someone has to patch it, which can be slow and uneven.

- Daybreak Initiative (auto-fixing vulnerabilities):
  - Intends to shift the industry from just finding problems to automatically fixing them.
  - Uses a set of tools and programs (not a single model) to detect and provide fixes. Example: the Codex Security Plugin scans code, simulates how it could be breached, and suggests specific changes to patch the vulnerability.
  - Includes partnerships (Daybreak Cyber Partners, Patch the Planet) where advanced models are used to find and fix bugs across many organizations, aiming for faster, automated remediation at scale.

Bottom line: traditional approaches emphasize locating problems and relying on humans to patch them; Daybreak aims to automate the detection-to-fix pipeline so vulnerabilities are fixed more quickly and broadly.

testCases.name: test_case_12
testCases.input: How do LLM evals differ from software tests in fixed vs. flexible output and multi-metric quality?
testCases.actualOutput:
Fixed vs. flexible output
- Traditional software: outputs are fixed and deterministic. Same input always yields the same exact output (e.g., 2 + 3 → 5). Tests are simple pass/fail assertions.
- LLMs: outputs are flexible and probabilistic. The same prompt can produce very different but valid responses (different words, lengths, phrasing). Correctness is semantic rather than exact-string, so simple assertion-based testing often fails.

Multi-metric quality (vs. single correctness)
- Traditional software: you mainly measure correctness (did it produce the expected value?).
- LLM-based applications: you must evaluate multiple dimensions, for example:
  - Correctness (is the answer factually right?)
  - Relevance (does the answer address the asked question? e.g., giving underfitting when asked about overfitting is incorrect/relevant)
  - Completeness (is the answer sufficiently thorough?)
  - Grounding (is the answer based on the intended data source, e.g., in a RAG system?)
- Multiple components (retriever, generator) can fail independently, so evaluation must consider component-level issues as well.

Consequences
- There is a grey area rather than binary pass/fail.
- Evaluation is costlier because it often requires text-level judgment; human annotation doesn’t scale, pushing toward automated approaches.

testCases.actualOutput:
Goals: non-blocking logging, durable & queryable storage, late-signal attachment, PII masking.

Recommended high-level schema (store in a structured data warehouse / observability tool like Langsmith):
- conversation_id — unique id for the whole conversation (used to link late signals).
- session_id / user_id — id for the user or session that started the conversation.
- turn_id — id for each turn within the conversation (one record per turn).
- role — who produced the text (user / bot / system).
- content — the textual content for the turn after PII masking.
- metadata — channel/source, model info, any flags (kept queryable).
- storage_reference — pointer or id in the warehouse/observability tool for durability/querying.

Non-blocking logging guidance:
- Log turns concurrently with the live conversation so logging does not increase end-user latency (keep logging non-blocking; conversation proceeds normally while logging happens in background).

Durability & queryability:
- Persist all records into a data warehouse / observability tool (e.g., Langsmith) in a structured way so you can fetch and query later.

Late-signal attachment:
- Store late signals (escalations, support emails, downstream outcomes) as separate records that reference conversation_id so they can be attached after the fact.
- Ensure the late-signal record includes the conversation_id so you can join/query the original conversation.

PII handling:
- Detect personal identifiable information in content (phone number, card number, date of birth, Aadhaar, etc.) and mask/blur it before storing.
- Only store the masked content in the warehouse/observability tool so teammates cannot extract raw PII later.
